Now Rule 405, methods of proof. 405(a): when evidence of a character trait is admissible, it may be proved by testimony about the person's reputation or by testimony in the form of an opinion. On cross-examination of the character witness, the court may allow an inquiry into relevant specific instances of the person's conduct.

So, on direct, reputation or opinion only. On cross, have you heard or do you know questions about specific acts, which test the witness's basis. Two limits from Michelson: the examiner needs a good-faith basis, and the examiner is stuck with the answer. No extrinsic proof of the act.
405(b): when a person's character or character trait is an essential element of a charge, claim, or defense, it may also be proved by relevant specific instances of the person's conduct.

405(b) is narrow. Character is an element in entrapment, where predisposition is at issue. In truth as a defense to defamation, when the statement was about character. In negligent entrustment. In child custody. And in sexually-violent-person commitment. But here is the trap: character is not an element of self-defense. The issue is the defendant's reasonable fear. So a victim's specific violent acts are not admissible under 405(b) to prove the victim's character. They might come in another way, for example to show what the defendant knew and feared, but not as character proof.
Another trap, Problem 3.16. A defendant who testifies, I wouldn't shoot anybody, makes herself a character witness, and may be crossed on past shootings.

The case. Michelson v. United States, 1948. A bribery defendant called five reputation witnesses. The prosecutor asked four of them whether they had heard of Michelson's 1920 arrest for receiving stolen goods.

Held: proper. A defendant who puts his reputation in issue opens it to cross-examination testing what the witness has heard. In the Court's words, it is not the man that he is, but the name that he has, that is at issue. The prosecutor had a good-faith basis, and the judge instructed the jury properly. Justice Rutledge dissented: the question itself plants the fact in the jury's mind.
Why Michelson matters: it is the 405(a) cross-examination rule. Back then, only reputation was allowed. Today opinion testimony is also allowed, so the question can be, do you know.

segments.ask: In an assault case, the defendant calls a witness to testify that the defendant has a reputation as peaceful. Proper? And can the prosecution respond?
segments.answer: Proper under 404(a)(2)(A), in reputation form under 405(a). The prosecution may rebut with reputation or opinion and may cross with have you heard questions with a good-faith basis.

segments.ask: The defendant claims self-defense and offers testimony that the victim had a reputation for violence. What can the prosecution now offer?
segments.answer: Rebuttal of the victim's trait, and evidence of the defendant's same trait, violence, under 404(a)(2)(B).

segments.ask: In a homicide case, the defendant offers an eyewitness who says the victim swung first. No character evidence. Can the prosecutor offer the victim's peacefulness?
segments.answer: Yes. Under 404(a)(2)(C), any evidence that the victim was the first aggressor opens the door to the victim's peacefulness in a homicide case.

segments.ask: In a self-defense case, the defendant wants to prove three specific prior fights the victim started, to prove the victim's violent character. Admissible under 405(b)?
segments.answer: No. Character is not an essential element of self-defense, so specific acts are not allowed under 405(b) to prove the victim's character.

segments.say: Traps. One: only the accused opens the door, and only in criminal cases. Two: direct is reputation or opinion only. Three: specific acts only on cross, with a good-faith basis, and the examiner takes the answer. Four: 404(a)(2)(B) opens the defendant's same trait. Five: 404(a)(2)(C) is homicide only, and triggered by any first-aggressor evidence. Six: character is not an element of self-defense.

Recap. 404(a)(2)(A): the defendant's own pertinent trait. (B): the victim's pertinent trait, subject to 412, opening the defendant's same trait. (C): homicide, victim's peacefulness to rebut first-aggressor evidence. 405(a): reputation or opinion; specific instances on cross. 405(b): specific instances when character is an essential element. Michelson: have you heard questions are proper.

segments.ask: List the five examples where character is an essential element under 405(b).
segments.answer: Entrapment predisposition, truth as a defense to defamation, negligent entrustment, custody, and sexually-violent-person commitment.

segments.ask: What two limits does Michelson put on have you heard questions?
segments.answer: A good-faith basis, and the examiner is stuck with the answer, with no extrinsic proof. Plus a proper instruction.

segments.ask: Quote Michelson's line about reputation.
segments.answer: It is not the man that he is, but the name that he has.

segments.say: Roadmap. Rule 406, what makes something habit rather than character, Halloran, Weil v. Seltzer, and the outline's character steps.

The exact rule. Rule 406: evidence of a person's habit or an organization's routine practice may be admitted to prove that on a particular occasion the person or organization acted in accordance with the habit or routine practice. The court may admit this evidence regardless of whether it is corroborated or whether there was an eyewitness.
Notice what that means. Habit is the one place you may reason from past behavior to conduct on this occasion. So the line between habit and character is critical.
Definition. Habit is a regular, specific, semi-automatic response to a specific recurring situation. Buckling a seatbelt every time you get in the car. The phrase: predictable and predictive.
Three things, all needed. Specific. Regular. Semi-automatic.

Occasional conduct is not enough. The outline's example is Halloran, testimony that a mechanic regularly heated Freon cans with an immersion coil. The point: the conduct must be regular, not occasional, to be habit.

And deliberate, morally charged conduct is usually character. Weil v. Seltzer, D.C. Circuit, 1989, a note case and a Fisher problem. An allergist treated a patient for over 20 years with pills he called antihistamines that were really prednisone, a steroid. Eight other long-term patients got the same treatment and the same description.

Held: the other patients' testimony was not habit evidence under 406. It was deliberate deception that varied by patient, and eight patients out of a large practice is not regular. It might fit 404(b), for example to show plan or intent. Why it matters: deliberate, morally charged conduct rarely qualifies as habit.

Why does the law trust habit but not character? Character is general, like being careful or honest. Habit is a specific, almost reflexive response, so it predicts behavior far better and invites less moral judgment.

segments.ask: A witness will testify the decedent always, every day for years, stopped and looked both ways at a particular railroad crossing. Habit?
segments.answer: Yes. A specific, regular, semi-automatic response to a recurring situation. Admissible under 406.

segments.ask: A witness will testify the plaintiff is a careful driver. Habit?
segments.answer: No. That is a general character trait, barred by 404(a)(1) in a civil case.

segments.ask: A doctor allegedly lied to many patients about their medication, varying the story for each. Habit?
segments.answer: No, under Weil v. Seltzer. Deliberate, varying, morally charged conduct is character, though it might come in under 404(b).

segments.say: The outline's character steps, six of them. Step one: is it offered to show action in character? If not, 404 does not apply, though 403 does. Step two: a propensity route exists only through 404(a)(2) in a criminal case once the accused opens the door, or 413 through 415 in sex cases. Step three: form. Reputation or opinion under 405(a). Specific acts only on cross of a character witness, or when character is an essential element under 405(b). Step four: under 404(b)(2), state the non-propensity chain inference by inference. MIMIC, motive, intent, absence of mistake, identity, common plan, is a memory aid, but the rule's list is longer and not exhaustive. Then Huddleston: proper purpose, 104(b) sufficiency, 403, a 105 instruction on request. In a criminal case, the prosecutor owes written notice under 404(b)(3). Step five: a witness's truthfulness goes to 607 through 609, not 404. Step six: habit under 406 is not character. Is the response specific, regular, and semi-automatic?

Recap. Rule 406: habit or routine practice may prove conduct on a particular occasion, with or without corroboration or an eyewitness. Specific, regular, semi-automatic. Halloran: occasional is not regular. Weil: deliberate, morally charged conduct is character.

segments.ask: What three qualities make conduct a habit?
segments.answer: Specific, regular, and semi-automatic: a response to a specific recurring situation.

segments.ask: Does habit evidence need corroboration or an eyewitness under 406?
segments.answer: No. It is admissible regardless of corroboration or an eyewitness.

segments.ask: What does MIMIC stand for, and what's the caveat?
segments.answer: Motive, intent, absence of mistake, identity, common plan. It is a memory aid; the rule's list is longer and not exhaustive.

segments.say: Roadmap. Rule 607, the two families of impeachment, Rule 610 on religion, and the critical question of when extrinsic evidence is allowed.
Rule 607: any party, including the party that called the witness, may attack the witness's credibility. The old voucher rule, that you vouch for your own witness and cannot impeach him, is gone.

Two families, from the slides. Family one: the witness is lying now. That covers contradiction, prior inconsistent statements, bias, and capacity. Family two: the witness is a liar. That covers 608(a) reputation and opinion, 608(b) specific acts, and 609 convictions.

Bias is never collateral, and may be proved extrinsically. That is Abel. Rule 610: evidence of a witness's religious beliefs or opinions is not admissible to attack or support the witness's credibility.
Now extrinsic evidence. Extrinsic means evidence other than the witness's own answers on cross: another witness, or a document. Mode by mode.

Bias and capacity: may be proved extrinsically. 608(b) specific acts: may not; cross only. A 609 conviction: may be proved extrinsically, by the record. A contradiction or an inconsistent statement on a collateral matter, one relevant only to contradict the witness, usually may not. Under the common-law collateral-matter principle, the witness's answer on such a point stands.

And a fine point: 608(b)'s bar on extrinsic evidence is absolute only when the sole purpose is to attack character for truthfulness. That comes from the Advisory Committee Note and Abel. If the evidence also shows bias, it can come in for bias.

segments.ask: A defense witness denies on cross that he is being paid by the defendant. Can the prosecution call another witness to prove the payments?
segments.answer: Yes. Bias is never collateral and may be proved extrinsically.

segments.ask: A witness says she wore a red coat on the day she saw the robbery. The opponent wants to call a witness to prove it was blue, solely to show she is wrong. Allowed?
segments.answer: Usually not. That is contradiction on a collateral matter, relevant only to contradict, so her answer stands.

segments.ask: May a party impeach its own witness?
segments.answer: Yes. Under Rule 607, any party, including the party that called the witness, may attack credibility.

segments.say: Recap. 607: any party may impeach. Two families: lying now, meaning contradiction, inconsistency, bias, capacity; and a liar, meaning 608(a), 608(b), and 609. 610 bars religion. Extrinsic proof: yes for bias, capacity, and 609; no for 608(b) and collateral contradictions.

segments.ask: Name the four modes in the witness is lying now family.
segments.answer: Contradiction, prior inconsistent statement, bias, and capacity.

segments.ask: Which impeachment mode is never collateral?
segments.answer: Bias.

segments.ask: Which rule bars attacking credibility with religious beliefs?
segments.answer: Rule 610.

segments.say: Roadmap. Rule 608(a) and (b) word for word, the five limits on 608(b), rehabilitation, and two cases: Whitmore and Abel.

The exact rule. Rule 608(a): a witness's credibility may be attacked or supported by testimony about the witness's reputation for having a character for truthfulness or untruthfulness, or by testimony in the form of an opinion about that character. But evidence of truthful character is admissible only after the witness's character for truthfulness has been attacked.

Rule 608(b): except for a criminal conviction under Rule 609, extrinsic evidence is not admissible to prove specific instances of a witness's conduct in order to attack or support the witness's character for truthfulness. But the court may, on cross-examination, allow them to be inquired into if they are probative of the character for truthfulness or untruthfulness of, one, the witness, or two, another witness whose character the witness being cross-examined has testified about.
Scope. 608 applies in civil and criminal cases, to every witness, and either side may start the attack.

Five limits on 608(b), all required. One: the act must be probative of truthfulness. Ask about the lie, not the underlying misconduct. Two: no extrinsic proof. Take the answer. Three: 403 discretion. Four: a good-faith basis, from Whitmore. Five: protection from harassment under Rule 611(a). And extrinsic evidence offered for another purpose, such as bias, is governed by 401 through 403 instead.

Rehabilitation. You may support truthful character only after an attack on character for truthfulness. Any one of three suffices. One, 608 opinion or reputation evidence of untruthfulness. Two, 608(b) acts. Three, 609 convictions. But bias is not such an attack, per the Advisory Committee Note. And a single contradiction usually is not, per Problems 4.6 and 4.7.

First case. United States v. Whitmore, D.C. Circuit, 2004. A gun case resting on one officer, Officer Soto. The defense offered three witnesses to testify to Soto's bad reputation for truthfulness and their opinion that he was untruthful. It also sought to cross Soto about lying regarding his suspended driver's license and about unpaid child support.

Held, in two parts. Excluding the 608(a) witnesses was within the judge's discretion, because their information was too remote or too narrow. But barring the 608(b) cross was an abuse of discretion. The questioner needs only a good-faith basis, not admissible proof, and lying about the license is probative of untruthfulness. And the error was not harmless, since the case rested on Soto.
Why Whitmore matters. 608(b) bars extrinsic proof, not questions.

Second case. United States v. Abel, 1984. A defense witness denied on cross that he and the defendant belonged to a secret prison gang whose members were sworn to lie, steal, or kill for one another. The prosecution then called a witness to prove the membership.

Held, by then-Justice Rehnquist for a unanimous Court: admissible. The membership showed bias, as well as untruthful character. Bias is not character evidence, is never collateral, and may be proved extrinsically.

Why Abel matters. Rule 608(b) bars extrinsic evidence only when its sole purpose is to prove character for truthfulness. Evidence admissible for one purpose is not excluded because it would be barred for another. That is Rule 105 again.

segments.ask: On cross, a lawyer asks a witness, isn't it true you lied on your job application? The witness denies it. Can the lawyer now offer the application?
segments.answer: No. 608(b) bars extrinsic evidence of specific acts to attack truthfulness. The lawyer is stuck with the answer.

segments.ask: On cross, can a lawyer ask a witness about a past assault, to show untruthfulness?
segments.answer: No. An assault is not probative of truthfulness. 608(b) reaches only acts probative of truthfulness or untruthfulness.

segments.ask: After opposing counsel shows a witness is the defendant's cousin, may the defendant call a witness to testify to the cousin's truthful character?
segments.answer: No. Bias is not an attack on character for truthfulness, so rehabilitation under 608(a) is not triggered.

segments.ask: A witness denies on cross that he and the defendant belong to a gang sworn to lie for each other. Can the prosecution prove membership extrinsically?
segments.answer: Yes, under Abel. It shows bias, which is never collateral.

segments.say: Traps. One: 608(b) is cross-only, with no extrinsic proof, but questions are allowed with a good-faith basis. Two: ask about the lie, not the misconduct. Three: truthful-character support only after an attack on character for truthfulness, not after bias. Four: 608(b) does not bar extrinsic evidence that also proves bias.

Recap. 608(a): reputation or opinion on truthfulness; support only after attack. 608(b): specific acts on cross only, if probative of truthfulness, no extrinsic proof except 609 convictions. Five limits: probative of truthfulness, no extrinsic proof, 403, good faith, 611(a). Whitmore: questions with a good-faith basis are allowed. Abel: bias may be proved extrinsically.

segments.ask: What are the three kinds of attack that trigger rehabilitation with truthful character?
segments.answer: 608 opinion or reputation, 608(b) acts, or 609 convictions.

segments.ask: Under 608(b)(2), whose truthfulness can you ask a character witness about?
segments.answer: Another witness whose character the witness being cross-examined has testified about.

segments.ask: What were the two holdings in Whitmore?
segments.answer: Excluding the 608(a) witnesses was within discretion; barring the 608(b) cross about lying regarding his license was an abuse of discretion.

segments.say: Roadmap. Rule 609's three tracks, the ten-year rule, pardons, juvenile adjudications, appeals, the comparison chart, crimen falsi, preservation under Luce and Ohler, and Brewer with the five Gordon factors.
Plain English. A witness's criminal record can be used to suggest the witness is not believable, with different tests depending on the crime and the witness.
The exact rule. Rule 609(a). To attack a witness's character for truthfulness by evidence of a criminal conviction, two tracks.

Track one, 609(a)(1), for a crime punishable by death or by imprisonment for more than one year in the convicting jurisdiction. That is, felonies. Two sub-rules. (A): the evidence must be admitted, subject to Rule 403, in a civil case or in a criminal case in which the witness is not a defendant. (B): the evidence must be admitted in a criminal case in which the witness is a defendant, if the probative value of the evidence outweighs its prejudicial effect to that defendant.

Track two, 609(a)(2), for any crime regardless of the punishment: the evidence must be admitted if the court can readily determine that establishing the elements of the crime required proving, or the witness's admitting, a dishonest act or false statement.

Let me give you the comparison chart in words. Dishonesty or false statement, any punishment: must be admitted, no 403. Felony, any witness except a criminal defendant: 403, excluded only if substantially outweighed. Felony, the criminal defendant: admitted only if probative value outweighs prejudicial effect. More than 10 years old, from the later of conviction or release: probative value must substantially outweigh prejudice, plus written notice.

Now 609(b), the ten-year limit. If more than 10 years have passed since the witness's conviction or release from confinement for it, whichever is later, the evidence is admissible only if its probative value, supported by specific facts and circumstances, substantially outweighs its prejudicial effect, and the proponent gives the adverse party reasonable written notice of the intent to use it.

609(c): a pardon, annulment, certificate of rehabilitation, or equivalent procedure bars use if it was based on a finding of rehabilitation and the person has not been convicted of a later felony, or if it was based on a finding of innocence.

609(d): juvenile adjudications are admissible only in a criminal case, only against a witness other than the defendant, only if an adult's conviction for that offense would be admissible to attack the adult's credibility, and only if admitting it is necessary to fairly determine guilt or innocence. Four onlys.
609(e): a conviction is admissible even if an appeal is pending. And evidence of the pendency is also admissible.

Nuances. What counts for the felony track is the maximum punishment, not the sentence imposed. Larceny, robbery, and drug crimes are generally not crimen falsi. The court looks at the elements, and if needed, the indictment, admitted facts, or jury instructions. That comes from the 2006 Advisory Committee Note. And 609(b)'s ten-year rule applies to crimen falsi too.

Preservation. Luce v. United States, 1984. After the court ruled in limine that his prior conviction could be used to impeach him, the defendant did not testify. Held: to preserve a challenge to an in limine 609 ruling, the defendant must testify. Otherwise the harm is wholly speculative.

Ohler v. United States, 2000. After an in limine ruling admitting her prior drug conviction, the defendant disclosed it herself on direct, to remove the sting. Held, by Chief Justice Rehnquist, five to four, Justice Souter dissenting: a defendant who preemptively introduces her own conviction on direct may not challenge its admission on appeal.
Put Luce and Ohler together: a defendant preserves a 609 objection only by testifying and letting the prosecution elicit the conviction.

The main case. United States v. Brewer, Eastern District of Tennessee, 1978. Charged with kidnapping and transporting a stolen car, Brewer sought to bar impeachment with a 1960 kidnapping conviction and three 1968 Ohio convictions, for rape and two assaults.

Held: 609(b) did not apply. The ten years run from the later of conviction or release, and he was released within ten years, including release from reconfinement for a parole violation on the kidnapping. So the court applied 609(a)(1)(B), using the Gordon factors. The kidnapping conviction was excluded: identical to the charged crime, and overkill. The other three were admitted.

The five Gordon factors. One, the nature of the crime; violence says little about veracity. Two, its recency and the witness's later history. Three, similarity to the charged crime, which weighs against admission. Four, the importance of the defendant's testimony, which weighs against admission. Five, the centrality of credibility, which weighs for admission.

segments.ask: A civil plaintiff testifies. The defense wants to impeach her with a two-year-old felony assault conviction. Which test?
segments.answer: 609(a)(1)(A): must be admitted, subject to 403.

segments.ask: A criminal defendant testifies. The prosecution offers a three-year-old misdemeanor perjury conviction. Which test?
segments.answer: 609(a)(2): perjury requires proving a false statement, so it must be admitted with no balancing.

segments.ask: The defendant was convicted of a felony 14 years ago and released 8 years ago. Does 609(b) apply?
segments.answer: No. Ten years runs from the later of conviction or release, so only 8 years have passed. Use 609(a).

segments.ask: A defendant charged with robbery has a prior robbery conviction. Which Gordon factor weighs most heavily against admission?
segments.answer: Similarity to the charged crime, which invites a propensity inference.

segments.ask: The court rules in limine that the defendant's prior can be used. The defendant decides not to testify. Can he appeal the ruling?
segments.answer: No. Under Luce, he must testify to preserve the challenge.

segments.say: Traps. One: maximum punishment, not the sentence imposed. Two: robbery, larceny, and drug crimes are generally not crimen falsi. Three: the clock runs from the later of conviction or release. Four: 609(b) applies to crimen falsi too. Five: the defendant track is straight balancing, with ties excluding. Six: juvenile adjudications never against the defendant.

Recap. 609(a)(1)(A): felonies against non-defendant witnesses, subject to 403. 609(a)(1)(B): felonies against a testifying defendant, if probative value outweighs prejudice to the defendant. 609(a)(2): dishonesty crimes, must be admitted. 609(b): over ten years, reverse 403 plus notice. 609(c) pardons, 609(d) juveniles, 609(e) appeals. Luce and Ohler on preservation. Brewer and the Gordon factors.

segments.ask: Name the five Gordon factors.
segments.answer: The nature of the crime; its recency and the witness's later history; similarity to the charged crime; the importance of the defendant's testimony; and the centrality of credibility.

segments.ask: State the four limits on juvenile adjudications under 609(d).
segments.answer: Only in a criminal case, only against a witness other than the defendant, only if an adult conviction would be admissible, and only if necessary to fairly determine guilt or innocence.

segments.ask: What did Ohler hold?
segments.answer: A defendant who preemptively introduces her own conviction on direct cannot challenge its admission on appeal.

segments.say: Roadmap. Rule 412's general bar, the three criminal exceptions, the civil test, the procedure, why the rule exists, prior false accusations, the asymmetry with 413 through 415, Olden v. Kentucky, and the impeachment steps.
Plain English. In sexual-misconduct cases, a victim's other sexual behavior and sexual predisposition stay out, with narrow exceptions.

The exact rule. Rule 412(a): in a civil or criminal proceeding involving alleged sexual misconduct, evidence offered to prove that a victim engaged in other sexual behavior, or offered to prove a victim's sexual predisposition, is not admissible.

412(b)(1), criminal cases. The court may admit three things. A: evidence of specific instances of a victim's sexual behavior, if offered to prove that someone other than the defendant was the source of semen, injury, or other physical evidence. B: evidence of specific instances of a victim's sexual behavior with respect to the person accused of the sexual misconduct, if offered by the defendant to prove consent, or if offered by the prosecutor. C: evidence whose exclusion would violate the defendant's constitutional rights.

412(b)(2), civil cases. The court may admit evidence offered to prove a victim's sexual behavior or sexual predisposition if its probative value substantially outweighs the danger of harm to any victim and of unfair prejudice to any party. That is the reverse 403 from day one. And the court may admit evidence of a victim's reputation only if the victim has placed it in controversy.

412(c), procedure. A party intending to offer such evidence must file a motion at least 14 days before trial, specifically describing the evidence and stating its purpose, serve it on all parties, and notify the victim. Before admitting the evidence, the court must conduct an in camera hearing, and the motion and record are sealed. Fourteen days for 412; fifteen days for 413 through 415. Watch that.

Why the rule? The slides explain the common law. It let defendants argue that past consent meant present consent, through the analogue of 404(a)(2)(B). And that unchastity showed untruthfulness, through the analogue of 608(b). Wigmore urged suspicion of complainants. Colb's response: once a woman swears she did not consent, her history has no real predictive force.

Prior false accusations. A prior false accusation of rape is not sexual behavior, so 412 does not reach it. The threshold is whether a jury could find the accusation was false. That is State v. Smith, Louisiana, 1999, which borrows the Huddleston standard. But ordinary 403 and 608(b) limits still apply.

The asymmetry with 413 through 415, from the slides. Why can the defendant's past sexual conduct come in while the victim's is shielded? The shield protects reporting and privacy, interests a past offender lacks. And a victim's history cuts both ways, while a defendant's prior rapes cut one way.

The case. Olden v. Kentucky, 1988. Olden claimed the complainant consented and that she invented the rape story to explain to Russell, her live-in partner, why she was getting out of another man's car. The trial court barred all evidence that she and Russell lived together.

Held: reversed, per curiam. The Confrontation Clause protects cross-examination designed to show a prototypical form of bias. Her testimony was central, and it was corroborated only by Russell, whose own bias the evidence would also show.
Why Olden matters: it is the model for 412(b)(1)(C). Exclusion that cuts off proof of bias violates the Constitution.

The outline's impeachment steps, five. One, name the theory: bias, contradiction, inconsistency, 608(a), 608(b), or 609. Two, apply its form-of-proof limits: opinion or reputation, cross only, or a record of conviction. Three, is extrinsic evidence allowed? Bias and non-collateral matters, yes; 608(b) character, no. Four, has character been attacked before rehabilitation? Five, 403, 611(a), and, in sex cases, 412.

segments.ask: In a rape prosecution, the defendant offers evidence that the victim had sex with another man the same night, to explain the source of semen. Admissible?
segments.answer: Potentially yes, under 412(b)(1)(A), after a 14-day motion and in camera hearing.

segments.ask: The defendant offers evidence of the victim's prior consensual sex with him, to prove consent. Admissible?
segments.answer: Potentially yes, under 412(b)(1)(B): specific instances with the accused, offered by the defendant to prove consent.

segments.ask: The defendant offers evidence the victim falsely accused another man of rape last year. Does 412 bar it?
segments.answer: No. A prior false accusation is not sexual behavior. The threshold is whether a jury could find it false, and 403 and 608(b) still apply.

segments.ask: In a civil sexual-harassment suit, the defense offers evidence of the plaintiff's sexual history. What test?
segments.answer: 412(b)(2): probative value must substantially outweigh harm to any victim and unfair prejudice to any party. Reputation only if the victim placed it in controversy.

segments.say: Traps. One: 412 covers civil and criminal cases. Two: criminal exceptions are three specific ones; civil is a reverse-403 balance. Three: 14 days' notice, in camera, sealed. Four: prior false accusations are outside 412. Five: the constitutional exception tracks Olden, bias.

Recap. 412(a) bars a victim's other sexual behavior and sexual predisposition. 412(b)(1): source of physical evidence, prior acts with the accused, and constitutional rights. 412(b)(2): civil reverse 403. 412(c): 14-day motion, in camera, sealed. Olden: bias cross is constitutionally protected.

segments.ask: What are the three criminal exceptions in 412(b)(1)?
segments.answer: Someone else as the source of semen, injury, or physical evidence; specific instances with the accused, offered by the defendant for consent or by the prosecutor; and evidence whose exclusion would violate the defendant's constitutional rights.

segments.ask: When can a victim's reputation come in under 412 in a civil case?
segments.answer: Only if the victim has placed it in controversy.

segments.ask: What theory of bias did Olden want to show?
segments.answer: That the complainant invented the rape to explain to her live-in partner, Russell, why she was getting out of another man's car.

segments.say: Cumulative quiz, days one and two. Out loud.

segments.ask: What makes the 404(b)(2) purposes different from true exceptions?
segments.answer: They are non-character routes, not exceptions to the propensity ban. The true exceptions are 404(a)(2), 404(a)(3), and 413 through 415.

segments.ask: Who must give notice under 404(b)(3), and what must it say?
segments.answer: The prosecutor in a criminal case, in writing, articulating the permitted purpose and the reasoning that supports it.

segments.ask: Under Huddleston, who decides whether the other act happened?
segments.answer: The jury. The judge asks only whether a jury could reasonably find it by a preponderance, under 104(b).

segments.ask: Stevens: what's the standard for reverse 404(b)?
segments.answer: Ordinary 401 similarity enough to suggest one person committed both, then 403.

segments.ask: The defendant in a fraud case calls a witness to say he is honest. Specific acts on direct?
segments.answer: No. Only reputation or opinion on direct under 405(a). Specific acts only on cross.

segments.ask: Which of these can be proved extrinsically: bias, a 608(b) lie, a 609 conviction?
segments.answer: Bias and the 609 conviction. Not the 608(b) lie.

segments.ask: A testifying criminal defendant's six-year-old felony burglary conviction. Test?
segments.answer: 609(a)(1)(B): probative value must outweigh prejudicial effect to the defendant.

segments.ask: Ten-year clock under 609(b) runs from what?
segments.answer: The later of conviction or release from confinement for it.

segments.ask: Notice periods: 412 versus 413 through 415?
segments.answer: 412 requires a motion at least 14 days before trial. 413 through 415 require disclosure at least 15 days before trial.

segments.ask: A testifying witness is impeached only with bias. Can the other side call a character witness to say he is truthful?
segments.answer: No. Bias is not an attack on character for truthfulness.

segments.ask: From day one: what did Collins teach about probability evidence?
segments.answer: It needs real data and independent factors. Made-up numbers and interrelated variables fail.

segments.ask: From day one: Rule 410 protects statements in plea talks with whom?
segments.answer: An attorney for the prosecuting authority, not police.

segments.say: That's day two. Tomorrow, hearsay. The biggest day of the course. Rest up.

days.title: Competency and hearsay: the definition, 801(d), 804, 803, and 807

segments.say: Day three. Hearsay day. First, rapid recall from the last two days.

segments.ask: What standard governs other-act evidence under Huddleston?
segments.answer: 104(b): whether a jury could reasonably find by a preponderance that the act occurred.

segments.ask: Trenkler's identity standard?
segments.answer: Characteristics sufficiently idiosyncratic to permit an inference of pattern, not prosaic commonalities.

segments.ask: When can the prosecution offer the defendant's violent character in a criminal case without the defendant offering his own?
segments.answer: When the defendant offers the alleged victim's violent character under 404(a)(2)(B). Then the prosecution may offer the defendant's same trait.

segments.ask: Habit: three qualities.
segments.answer: Specific, regular, and semi-automatic.

segments.ask: Michelson: what can a prosecutor ask a defendant's reputation witness?
segments.answer: Have you heard questions about relevant specific acts, with a good-faith basis, and the examiner is stuck with the answer.

segments.ask: 608(b): questions or extrinsic proof?
segments.answer: Questions on cross only, if probative of truthfulness. No extrinsic proof.

segments.ask: 609(a)(2): which crimes, and what test?
segments.answer: Crimes whose elements required proving or admitting a dishonest act or false statement. Must be admitted, no balancing.

segments.ask: Name 412's three criminal exceptions.
segments.answer: Another source of semen, injury, or physical evidence; specific instances with the accused; and constitutionally required evidence.

segments.ask: Rule 403's six dangers.
segments.answer: Unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay, wasting time, needless cumulative evidence.

segments.ask: Peña-Rodriguez's three elements.
segments.answer: Clear racial bias, in a criminal case, relied on to convict.

segments.say: Good. Now competency, then hearsay.
Roadmap. Who may testify. Rules 601, 602, 603, 605, and 606(a), the history, child witnesses, and how competency relates to hearsay.

Rule 601: every person is competent to be a witness unless the rules provide otherwise. But in a civil case, state law governs the witness's competency regarding a claim or defense for which state law supplies the rule of decision.

Rule 602: a witness may testify to a matter only if evidence is introduced sufficient to support a finding that the witness has personal knowledge of the matter. That is a 104(b) question. And the personal-knowledge rule does not apply to an expert's opinion under Rule 703.
Rule 603: before testifying, a witness must give an oath or affirmation to testify truthfully.
And two people may not testify. Rule 605: the presiding judge. Rule 606(a): a juror, before the other jurors at the trial.

History. The old rules barred parties, spouses, interested persons, felons, atheists, and non-white persons. All gone. Today competency mostly concerns young children. The questions: can the child perceive and remember, communicate, understand the duty to tell the truth, and answer on cross? And 18 U.S.C. section 3509(c) presumes children competent.
The slides tie it together. Competency asks whether this witness can be tested by cross. Hearsay asks whether this statement can be.

segments.ask: A witness testifies to what she heard was going on next door, but never saw or heard it herself. What's the objection?
segments.answer: Lack of personal knowledge under Rule 602.

segments.ask: In a federal diversity case on a state-law claim, which law governs witness competency?
segments.answer: State law, under Rule 601.

segments.say: Recap. 601: everyone is competent, with state law governing in civil cases where state law supplies the rule of decision. 602: personal knowledge, sufficient to support a finding, not required for expert opinion. 603: oath or affirmation. 605: not the judge. 606(a): not a juror at the trial.

segments.ask: Which rule exempts experts from personal knowledge?
segments.answer: Rule 703, noted in Rule 602.

segments.ask: What does 18 U.S.C. section 3509(c) do?
segments.answer: It presumes children competent.

segments.ask: Competency versus hearsay, in the slides' words?
segments.answer: Competency asks whether this witness can be tested by cross. Hearsay asks whether this statement can be.

segments.say: Roadmap. Rules 801(a), 801(c), and 802 word for word, the four testimonial capacities, why purpose controls, and the categories of not-hearsay.
The exact rules. Rule 801(a): statement means a person's oral assertion, written assertion, or nonverbal conduct, if the person intended it as an assertion.

Rule 801(c): hearsay means a statement that, two things. First, the declarant does not make while testifying at the current trial or hearing. Second, a party offers in evidence to prove the truth of the matter asserted in the statement.
Rule 802: hearsay is not admissible unless any of the following provides otherwise: a federal statute, these rules, or other rules prescribed by the Supreme Court.

Why exclude hearsay? The four testimonial capacities. Perception, memory, narration, and sincerity. Did she see it right? Does she remember it right? Is she saying what she means? Is she telling the truth? Cross-examination tests all four in a live witness. Hearsay leaves the declarant's capacities untested. The founding example: Sir Walter Raleigh's trial, convicted on Cobham's confession without being able to confront Cobham.

A trap right away. A witness repeating her own earlier words is still hearsay. If the witness says on the stand, I told my sister the light was red, and it is offered to prove the light was red, that earlier statement was not made while testifying at the current trial. Hearsay.
The golden rule from the slides: you can never answer the question, is this hearsay, without knowing the proponent's purpose.
Now the categories that are not hearsay, because they are not offered for their truth.

One, effect on the listener. Words offered to show notice, motive, or reasonable fear. The slides' example: Shelley Winters's marriage demand in A Place in the Sun, offered for its effect on the man who heard it, to show his motive. Or a complaint to a supervisor, offered to show the employer had notice.
Two, verbal acts. Words that have legal effect themselves: the words of a contract, threats, defamation. We care that they were said, not whether they are true.

Three, nonassertive conduct. Conduct not intended as an assertion. Santiago failing to pack. The sea captain who inspected a ship and then sailed on it with his family. The paramedics' silence. These are offered to prove what the actor believed, but the actor did not intend to assert anything, so under 801(a), there is no statement.
Four, involuntary exclamations. Ouch is not an assertion.
Five, words offered as circumstantial evidence of knowledge. A child's accurate description of the defendant's room. Drug recipes showing know-how.
Six, machine output. A machine is not a person, so it cannot make a statement.

Now the flip side. Conduct intended as an assertion is a statement. Pointing at a fleeing car, which says, that one. Or Minister Gummer eating beef for the press, which said, British beef is safe. And an implied or indirect assertion, offered for the belief behind it, if the speaker intended to communicate that belief, is hearsay. The outline's example: planning my retirement home, offered to show the speaker was not suicidal.
Two more basics. Rule 805: hearsay within hearsay is admissible only if each layer fits an exception. And the two justifications behind every exception, per the slides: necessity and trustworthiness.

segments.ask: In a contract case, the plaintiff testifies the defendant said, I accept your offer. Hearsay?
segments.answer: No. Words of acceptance are a verbal act with legal effect, not offered for their truth.

segments.ask: To show the defendant had reason to fear the victim, the defendant testifies that a friend told him the victim carried a gun. Hearsay?
segments.answer: No, if offered for its effect on the listener, to show the defendant's reasonable fear, not that the victim actually carried a gun.

segments.ask: A witness testifies, I told the officer the car was speeding, offered to prove the car was speeding. Hearsay?
segments.answer: Yes. Repeating her own out-of-court statement is still hearsay.

segments.ask: At a lineup, the victim points to the defendant. Is that pointing a statement?
segments.answer: Yes. Conduct intended as an assertion is a statement under 801(a). Whether it is hearsay depends on purpose, and an identification may fall under 801(d)(1)(C).

segments.say: Traps. One: purpose controls. Always name the purpose. Two: the declarant's intent to assert controls whether conduct is a statement. Three: a witness's own prior statement can be hearsay. Four: machine output is not hearsay, but a human-entered record is.

Recap. 801(a): a person's oral, written, or nonverbal assertion, intended as an assertion. 801(c): not made while testifying, offered for its truth. 802: inadmissible unless a statute, the rules, or Supreme Court rules provide otherwise. Not hearsay: effect on the listener, verbal acts, nonassertive conduct, involuntary exclamations, circumstantial proof of knowledge, machine output.

segments.ask: Name the four testimonial capacities.
segments.answer: Perception, memory, narration, and sincerity.

segments.ask: What are the two justifications behind every hearsay exception?
segments.answer: Necessity and trustworthiness.

segments.ask: What does Rule 805 require?
segments.answer: Each layer of hearsay within hearsay must fit an exception.

episodes.title: Implied assertions: Wright v. Tatham, Bridges, and Zenni

segments.say: Roadmap. Three note cases that show how the common law and the Federal Rules handle implied assertions and circumstantial knowledge.
Wright v. Doe d. Tatham, England, 1837. To prove a testator was sane, the will's supporters offered letters written to him by acquaintances, who addressed him as a man of normal understanding.
Held: excluded. The letters were treated as the writers' implied statements that he was sane, and so as hearsay.

Why it matters: this is the common-law view of implied assertions. And the Federal Rules reject it. Rule 801(a) defines a statement by the declarant's intent to assert. The letter writers did not intend to assert, he is sane.
United States v. Zenni, Eastern District of Kentucky, 1980. While agents searched premises for illegal bookmaking, they answered the phone. Unknown callers gave instructions for placing bets.

Held: not hearsay under the Federal Rules. The callers did not intend to assert that the premises were a betting operation, so their words were not offered for the truth of anything they asserted. Why it matters: Zenni is the Federal Rules' answer to Wright v. Tatham. Implied assertions are not statements.

Bridges v. State, Wisconsin, 1945. A seven-year-old said a stranger in a soldier's uniform took her to his room in a boarding house and assaulted her. Hours later she described the house and the room in detail to her mother and police. The details matched the defendant's room.

Held: admissible. The descriptions were offered as circumstantial evidence of what she knew, not to prove what the room looked like. Why it matters: words can prove knowledge the declarant could only have gained by being there. The words are true or false, it doesn't matter; what matters is that she knew details she could only know from being in that room.

segments.ask: A caller to a suspected drug house asks, can I get two bags tonight? Offered to show the house sold drugs. Hearsay under the FRE?
segments.answer: No, under the Zenni approach. The caller did not intend to assert that the house sold drugs, so it is not a statement offered for its truth.

segments.ask: Did the Federal Rules adopt or reject the Wright v. Tatham view of implied assertions?
segments.answer: Rejected. 801(a) defines a statement by the declarant's intent to assert.

segments.ask: Why was the child's description in Bridges not hearsay?
segments.answer: It was circumstantial evidence of her knowledge of the room, which she could only have gained by being there, not offered for the truth of the description.

segments.say: Roadmap. The five kinds of opposing-party statements, the bootstrapping rule, the 2024 successor sentence, no personal knowledge requirement, adoption by silence and the Miranda cases, and Mahlandt.
Plain English. Anything a party said can be used against that party. Plus statements the party adopted, authorized, or that its agents or coconspirators made.
The exact rule. Rule 801(d)(2). A statement is not hearsay if it is offered against an opposing party and is one of five things.
A: made by the party in an individual or representative capacity.
B: one the party manifested that it adopted or believed to be true.
C: made by a person whom the party authorized to make a statement on the subject.
D: made by the party's agent or employee on a matter within the scope of that relationship and while it existed.
E: made by the party's coconspirator during and in furtherance of the conspiracy.

Then the bootstrapping sentence. The statement must be considered, but does not by itself establish the declarant's authority under C, the existence or scope of the relationship under D, or the existence of the conspiracy or participation in it under E.

And the 2024 successor sentence. If a party's claim, defense, or potential liability is directly derived from a declarant or the declarant's principal, a statement that would be admissible against the declarant or the principal under this rule is also admissible against the party.

The successor sentence explained, from the 2024 Advisory Committee Note. A party who stands in the shoes of a declarant or the declarant's principal gets no better position on hearsay than they had. An estate suing on the decedent's claim takes the decedent's statements. So do an assignee, and a trustee pursuing the debtor's claims. But the sentence does not reach a statement made after the rights or obligations were transferred, or one admissible against an agent but not against the principal, such as one made after the employment ended.

Nuances. No personal knowledge requirement, and no against-interest requirement. That is Mahlandt. Opinions are fine. The justification is the adversary system: a party cannot complain she was unable to cross-examine herself.

Adoption by silence. Four elements, all required. One, the party heard and understood the statement. Two, the party was free to respond. Three, the circumstances naturally called for a denial. Four, the party did not deny.

And the constitutional limits on silence. Doyle v. Ohio, 1976. Defendants who stayed silent after Miranda warnings were cross-examined at trial about why they had not told police their exculpatory story. Held: using post-Miranda silence to impeach violates due process. Silence after the warnings is insolubly ambiguous, and the warnings implicitly promise silence will carry no penalty. So it is likely not usable as an adoption either. But pre-arrest and pre-Miranda silence may be used to impeach: Jenkins, and Fletcher v. Weir. And non-custodial silence may be used substantively: Salinas, a plurality.

Related Week 7 reading. Statements taken in violation of Miranda, Harris v. New York, 1971, or of the Sixth Amendment right to counsel, Kansas v. Ventris, 2009, may impeach a testifying defendant, even though they are inadmissible substantively. And post-Miranda silence may not be used as substantive evidence either, such as to prove sanity: Wainwright v. Greenfield, 1986.

The case. Mahlandt v. Wild Canid Survival and Research Center, Eighth Circuit, 1978. No one saw how a child was hurt near a chained wolf named Sophie. Poos, the Center's director of education, left a note saying Sophie bit a child, and told the president so. Board minutes later referred to the incident of Sophie biting the child.

Held: personal knowledge is not required under 801(d)(2). Poos's statements came in against Poos under A, and against the Center under D, as an agent's statements within the scope of his employment. The board minutes came in against the Center, but not against Poos. Why it matters: admissibility under 801(d)(2) is party-specific. And statements within an organization, like a note to the boss, count.

segments.ask: The defendant's truck driver, while on the job, tells a police officer at the scene, I was going too fast. Admissible against the trucking company?
segments.answer: Yes, under 801(d)(2)(D): an employee's statement on a matter within the scope of employment while it existed.

segments.ask: The same driver says it a week after being fired. Admissible against the company?
segments.answer: No, not under D. The relationship no longer existed.

segments.ask: At a party, someone says to the defendant, you stole that car, didn't you? The defendant laughs and walks away. Adoptive admission?
segments.answer: Possibly, under 801(d)(2)(B), if he heard and understood, was free to respond, the circumstances naturally called for denial, and he did not deny.

segments.ask: After Miranda warnings, the defendant says nothing when an officer accuses him. Can the prosecution use his silence?
segments.answer: No. Under Doyle, post-Miranda silence may not be used to impeach, and likely not as an adoption.

segments.ask: The executor of an estate sues on the decedent's contract claim. Before death, the decedent said, I never delivered the goods. Admissible against the estate?
segments.answer: Yes, under the 2024 successor sentence. The estate's claim is directly derived from the declarant.

segments.say: Traps. One: 801(d)(2) statements must be offered against the party who made them. You cannot offer your own statement. Two: no personal knowledge or against-interest requirement. Three: the statement alone cannot establish authority, agency, or conspiracy. Four: agency statements must be made while the relationship existed. Five: Doyle bars post-Miranda silence.

Recap. 801(d)(2): A party's own statement; B adopted; C authorized; D agent or employee within scope while employed; E coconspirator during and in furtherance. The statement is considered but not sufficient alone. 2024: successors take the declarant's statements. Mahlandt: no personal knowledge needed; admissibility is party-specific.

segments.ask: Name the five types of opposing-party statements.
segments.answer: Party's own; adopted; authorized; agent or employee within scope while the relationship existed; coconspirator during and in furtherance.

segments.ask: Four elements of adoption by silence?
segments.answer: Heard and understood, free to respond, circumstances naturally called for denial, and no denial.

segments.ask: In Mahlandt, against whom were the board minutes admissible?
segments.answer: Against the Center, but not against Poos.

segments.say: Roadmap. The coconspirator rule in detail, Bourjaily, and the 1997 amendment.

For a coconspirator statement under 801(d)(2)(E), the judge must find, by a preponderance under 104(a), three things. One, a conspiracy existed that included the declarant and the defendant. Two, the statement was made during the conspiracy. Three, it was in furtherance of the conspiracy.

The judge may consider the statement itself, but needs some independent evidence. That is Bourjaily plus the 1997 amendment, which added the sentence that the statement alone does not establish the conspiracy.
No conspiracy charge is needed. A joint venture suffices. And confessions to police almost never qualify, because confessing to police is not in furtherance of the conspiracy.
The case. Bourjaily v. United States, 1987. Lonardo's recorded calls with an FBI informant described a gentleman friend who would buy cocaine. Bourjaily took delivery, with 20,000 dollars in his car.

Held: preliminary facts under 801(d)(2)(E) are decided under 104(a) by a preponderance, and the court may consider the statements themselves. That displaced the old Glasser bootstrapping bar, which had required independent evidence. Justice Blackmun dissented: the exemption rests on agency, which should require independent proof.
Why Bourjaily matters: 104(a), not 104(b) conditional relevance, governs hearsay foundations.

segments.ask: After arrest, a coconspirator tells police, my partner planned it all. Admissible against the partner under 801(d)(2)(E)?
segments.answer: No. A confession to police is not during and in furtherance of the conspiracy.

segments.ask: One drug dealer tells another, the boss will pay you Friday, during an ongoing operation. Can the judge consider that statement in deciding whether the boss was part of the conspiracy?
segments.answer: Yes, under Bourjaily, but after the 1997 amendment, the statement alone is not enough. There must be some independent evidence.

segments.ask: Must the defendant be charged with conspiracy for 801(d)(2)(E) to apply?
segments.answer: No. No conspiracy charge is needed; a joint venture suffices.

segments.say: Recap. The judge decides conspiracy, during, and in furtherance by a preponderance under 104(a), may consider the statement, but needs some independent evidence. Bourjaily displaced Glasser's bootstrapping bar. Confessions to police almost never qualify.

segments.ask: What case did Bourjaily displace, and on what point?
segments.answer: Glasser, which barred bootstrapping by considering the statement itself.

segments.ask: What did Bourjaily take delivery with?
segments.answer: 20,000 dollars in his car.

episodes.title: Prior statements of a testifying witness: 801(d)(1), 613, and 612

segments.say: Roadmap. Rule 801(d)(1) A, B, and C, Rule 613(a) and (b), the December 2026 amendment, impeachment versus substantive use, three cases, Barrett, Tome, and Owens, and Rule 612 on refreshing memory.
The exact rule. Rule 801(d)(1). A statement is not hearsay if the declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination about a prior statement, and the statement is one of three things.
A: is inconsistent with the declarant's testimony and was given under penalty of perjury at a trial, hearing, or other proceeding, or in a deposition.

B: is consistent with the declarant's testimony and is offered, one, to rebut an express or implied charge that the declarant recently fabricated it or acted from a recent improper influence or motive in so testifying; or two, to rehabilitate the declarant's credibility as a witness when attacked on another ground.
C: identifies a person as someone the declarant perceived earlier.

Now the important amendment. Rule 801(d)(1)(A) changes on December 1, 2026, nine days before your final on December 10. The Supreme Court adopted the amendment on April 8, 2026. Unless Congress acts, it governs proceedings commenced after December 1, 2026, and, as far as just and practicable, pending ones. The new text of A simply says: is inconsistent with the declarant's testimony. The requirement that the statement was given under penalty of perjury at a proceeding or deposition is gone.

The effect, per the Committee Note. A prior inconsistent statement of a witness who testifies and is subject to cross about it is substantive evidence even if unsworn. So no limiting instruction is needed, and inconsistent and consistent statements are treated alike. The Committee reasoned that delayed cross under oath allays the hearsay concerns, and that the old rule was unduly narrow, of use mainly to prosecutors with grand jury testimony. Unchanged: 613(b) still governs extrinsic proof. 403 handles difficulties of proof. And the rule governs admissibility, not sufficiency.

For the exam. Fisher, 2022, and the Class 12 and 13 slides teach the old rule. Ask Professor Hornzell which version the final uses. Until then, for an unsworn prior inconsistent statement, give both results. Under the old rule: impeachment only. Under the amended rule: substantive evidence.

Now Rule 613. 613(a): when examining a witness about the witness's prior statement, a party need not show it or disclose its contents to the witness. But the party must, on request, show it or disclose its contents to an adverse party's attorney.

613(b), as amended in 2024: unless the court orders otherwise, extrinsic evidence of a witness's prior inconsistent statement may not be admitted until after the witness is given an opportunity to explain or deny the statement and an adverse party is given an opportunity to examine the witness about it. This does not apply to an opposing party's statement under 801(d)(2).

The core contrast: 613 impeaches; 801(d)(1)(A) is substantive. Under the old rule, an unsworn statement to police is impeachment only, so counsel may not argue it as proof. That's from the slides, citing Troisi. Extrinsic proof of an inconsistent statement is allowed under 613(b) on a non-collateral point. Under the 2026 amendment, that statement would also come in substantively.

Case one. United States v. Barrett, First Circuit, 1976. Witness Adams testified that Barrett admitted taking part in a stamp theft. Barrett offered two witnesses who heard Adams say later that he knew Barrett was not involved.

Held: exclusion was error. The statements were admissible to impeach Adams as inconsistent under 613, not for their truth. Their vagueness went to weight. Why it matters: inconsistent statements impeach even when they cannot come in substantively. And note: Barrett let the 613(b) foundation come at any time. Since December 1, 2024, it must come first, unless the court orders otherwise.

Case two. Tome v. United States, 1995. The defense claimed a six-year-old fabricated abuse allegations against her father so she could stay with her mother. The prosecution offered six witnesses who recounted her later statements describing the abuse.

Held, by Justice Kennedy, five to four: 801(d)(1)(B) admits consistent statements only if made before the alleged motive to fabricate arose. Why it matters: post-motive repetition does not rebut a charge of fabrication. Repeating a lie doesn't make it true. And the 2014 amendment added B(ii), rehabilitation on other grounds, such as a charge of faulty memory.
Case three. United States v. Owens, 1988. A beaten prison counselor identified Owens from a photo array. At trial, he could not remember seeing his attacker.

Held: neither the Confrontation Clause nor 801(d)(1)(C) was violated. The Clause guarantees, quote, an opportunity for effective cross-examination, not cross-examination that is effective in whatever way, and to whatever extent, the defense might wish. That quotes Delaware v. Fensterer. Why it matters: memory loss does not make a testifying witness unavailable for cross. And C admits an identification even if the witness now cannot remember, or misidentifies in court.

Now Rule 612 versus 803(5). Anything may refresh memory: a document, a photo, a song. The witness reads silently and then testifies from memory. And the adverse party may inspect the writing, cross on it, and introduce relevant parts. A recorded recollection, by contrast, comes in for its truth only with the 803(5) foundation, which we'll cover soon.

Rule 612 gives those options for a writing used to refresh while testifying, and for one used before testifying if the court decides justice requires it. In a criminal case, 18 U.S.C. section 3500 controls where it applies. The court cuts unrelated matter after reviewing in camera. If a writing is withheld, the court may issue any appropriate order. If the prosecution does not comply in a criminal case, the court must strike the testimony or, if justice so requires, declare a mistrial.

segments.ask: At trial, a witness says the light was green. Last year, in a sworn deposition, he said it was red. Under the rule in effect before December 2026, can the deposition be used to prove the light was red?
segments.answer: Yes. It is inconsistent, given under penalty of perjury in a deposition, and he testifies subject to cross, so 801(d)(1)(A) makes it substantive.

segments.ask: Same, but his earlier statement was an unsworn statement to a police officer. Give both results.
segments.answer: Under the old rule, impeachment only under 613, not substantive. Under the amendment effective December 1, 2026, it is substantive evidence because the witness testifies and is subject to cross.

segments.ask: The defense says the witness made up her story after she was promised leniency in March. The prosecution offers her consistent statement from April. Admissible under 801(d)(1)(B)(i)?
segments.answer: No. Under Tome, the consistent statement must predate the alleged motive.

segments.ask: A witness identified the defendant at a lineup but now testifies she cannot remember the attacker. Can the lineup identification come in?
segments.answer: Yes, under 801(d)(1)(C) and Owens. Memory loss does not make her unavailable for cross.

segments.ask: A party wants to prove a witness's prior inconsistent statement with another witness. Under 613(b) after 2024, what must happen first?
segments.answer: Unless the court orders otherwise, the witness must first be given a chance to explain or deny it, and the adverse party a chance to examine the witness about it.

segments.say: Traps. One: under the old rule, 801(d)(1)(A) requires the prior statement to be under penalty of perjury at a proceeding or deposition. A police interview fails. Two: the amendment, effective December 1, 2026, removes that requirement. Give both results. Three: Tome's pre-motive requirement for B(i). Four: 613(b) foundation now comes first. Five: 613(b) does not apply to opposing-party statements.

Recap. 801(d)(1)(A): inconsistent, and under the pre-2026 rule, sworn at a proceeding or deposition. B: consistent, to rebut recent fabrication or improper motive, if pre-motive under Tome, or to rehabilitate on another ground. C: identification. 613(a): need not show the witness; must show opposing counsel on request. 613(b): extrinsic proof after a chance to explain or deny. Barrett, Tome, Owens. 612: refreshing memory.

segments.ask: What three things are listed in 801(d)(1)?
segments.answer: A, prior inconsistent statements; B, prior consistent statements to rebut fabrication or rehabilitate; C, prior identifications.

segments.ask: What quotation from Owens, borrowed from Fensterer, describes the right to cross?
segments.answer: An opportunity for effective cross-examination, not cross-examination that is effective in whatever way, and to whatever extent, the defense might wish.

segments.ask: Under 612, when may an adverse party inspect a writing used to refresh memory before testifying?
segments.answer: If the court decides justice requires it. For a writing used while testifying, the adverse party is entitled to it.

episodes.title: Unavailability and former testimony: Rules 804(a) and 804(b)(1)

segments.say: Roadmap. The five grounds of unavailability, the procurement exception, the former-testimony exception, Volland-Golden, and Salerno with DiNapoli.

Rule 804 exceptions require that the declarant be unavailable. So first, prove unavailability under 804(a). Five grounds. The declarant: one, is exempted from testifying by a court ruling on privilege. Two, refuses to testify despite a court order. Three, testifies to not remembering the subject matter. Four, cannot be present or testify because of death or a then-existing infirmity, physical illness, or mental illness. Five, is absent and the proponent has not been able, by process or other reasonable means, to procure the declarant's attendance, or, for the exceptions in (b)(2), (3), and (4), the declarant's attendance or testimony.
The catch. A declarant is not unavailable if the statement's proponent procured or wrongfully caused the unavailability in order to prevent the declarant from attending or testifying.
Notice ground three. A witness who testifies to not remembering is unavailable for 804. But under Owens, a witness with memory loss is still available for cross under 801(d)(1). Different purposes.

Now 804(b)(1), former testimony. Testimony that was given as a witness at a trial, hearing, or lawful deposition, whether given during the current proceeding or a different one, and is now offered against a party who had, or, in a civil case, whose predecessor in interest had, an opportunity and similar motive to develop it by direct, cross-, or redirect examination.

Case. Volland-Golden v. City of Chicago, Northern District of Illinois, 2015. Volland was acquitted of resisting and battering two officers. He then sued them under section 1983 and died. His sister, continuing the suit, offered his testimony from the criminal trial.

Held: admissible. The State was the officers' predecessor in interest, sharing a similar stake. And the State had a similar motive to discredit Volland: the same events and issues, a similar strategy, and even higher criminal stakes. Why it matters: predecessor in interest applies only in civil cases, and asks about shared stakes and motive.

Cited in Volland-Golden: United States v. Salerno, 1992, and United States v. DiNapoli, Second Circuit en banc, 1993. Grand jury witnesses who had testified favorably to the defendants invoked the Fifth Amendment at trial. The defense offered their grand jury testimony under 804(b)(1).

Held: Salerno: the similar-motive requirement applies to the government too. There is no adversarial fairness shortcut. DiNapoli, on remand: similar motive means a substantially similar interest at a similar stage, and the prosecutors lacked it at the grand jury.

segments.ask: A witness who testified at a preliminary hearing, and was cross-examined by the defendant, has since died. The prosecution offers the testimony at trial. Admissible under the hearsay rules?
segments.answer: Yes, under 804(b)(1). He is unavailable by death, and the defendant had an opportunity and similar motive to cross.

segments.ask: The defendant offers grand jury testimony favorable to him from a witness who now takes the Fifth. The government objects it had no similar motive at the grand jury. Who wins under Salerno and DiNapoli?
segments.answer: Likely the government. Similar motive applies to the government too, and DiNapoli found prosecutors lacked a substantially similar motive at the grand jury stage.

segments.ask: The prosecution sends its key witness on a long vacation abroad so he cannot testify, then offers his former testimony. Is he unavailable?
segments.answer: No. A proponent who procured the unavailability to prevent testimony cannot claim it.

segments.say: Recap. 804(a): privilege, refusal despite order, lack of memory, death or illness, absence despite process or reasonable means; not if the proponent procured it. 804(b)(1): former testimony against a party, or in civil cases a predecessor in interest, with an opportunity and similar motive. Volland-Golden: the State as predecessor. Salerno and DiNapoli: similar motive binds the government.

segments.ask: Name the five grounds of unavailability.
segments.answer: Privilege, refusal despite a court order, lack of memory, death or infirmity, and absence despite process or other reasonable means.

segments.ask: Does predecessor in interest apply in criminal cases?
segments.answer: No. Only in civil cases.

segments.ask: What did DiNapoli say similar motive means?
segments.answer: A substantially similar interest at a similar stage.

episodes.title: Dying declarations, statements against interest, forfeiture, and Rule 806

segments.say: Roadmap. 804(b)(2), (3), and (6), the 2024 corroboration amendment, Rule 806, and three cases: Shepard, Williamson, and Gray.

804(b)(2), the dying declaration. Four elements. One, in a prosecution for homicide or in a civil case. Two, a statement the declarant made while believing the declarant's death to be imminent. Three, about its cause or circumstances. Four, the declarant is unavailable. Notice: the declarant need not actually die, but must be unavailable. And not in non-homicide criminal cases.

804(b)(3), the statement against interest. A statement that a reasonable person in the declarant's position would have made only if the person believed it to be true because, when made, it was so contrary to the declarant's proprietary or pecuniary interest, or had so great a tendency to invalidate the declarant's claim against someone else or to expose the declarant to civil or criminal liability. And in a criminal case, if offered as one that tends to expose the declarant to criminal liability, it must be supported by corroborating circumstances that clearly indicate its trustworthiness, after considering the totality of circumstances under which it was made and any evidence that supports or undermines it. That last clause came in 2024.

That corroboration requirement is Rule 804(b)(3)(B). The 2024 Advisory Committee Note explains it. The court must weigh both the circumstances of the statement, such as timing, spontaneity, and the declarant's likely motives, and any evidence supporting or undermining it, such as evidence placing a third-party confessor near the crime. Independent evidence is relevant but not necessarily dispositive.
The slides' subjective versus objective contrast. Dying declarations and excited utterances look to the declarant's actual state of mind. Statements against interest use a reasonable person.

804(b)(6), forfeiture by wrongdoing. A statement offered against a party that wrongfully caused, or acquiesced in wrongfully causing, the declarant's unavailability as a witness, and did so intending that result.

United States v. Gray, Fourth Circuit, 2005. The defendant killed her husband a week before he was to testify against her on assault charges. In her later insurance-fraud trial, she forfeited her hearsay objection to his statements. Notice: forfeiture applied even in a different trial. The proponent proves the wrongdoing and the intent by a preponderance under 104(a), per the 1997 Advisory Committee Note.

Rule 806. Once a hearsay statement, or a statement under 801(d)(2)(C), (D), or (E), has been admitted, the declarant's credibility may be attacked, and then supported, by any evidence that would be admissible if the declarant had testified. And the 613(b) foundation is not required, because the declarant isn't there to explain or deny.
Case one. Shepard v. United States, 1933. Two days after collapsing, Mrs. Shepard told her nurse, Dr. Shepard has poisoned me. She improved, relapsed, and died weeks later.

Held: not a dying declaration. She lacked a settled hopeless expectation of imminent death. Nor was it admissible as state of mind, because it looked backward to another person's act. Why it matters: the foundation for imminent death must be shown, and 803(3) excludes backward-looking memory.
Case two. Williamson v. United States, 1994. Harris was arrested with 19 kilograms of cocaine. He told an agent it belonged to Williamson. Harris refused to testify at Williamson's trial.

Held: 804(b)(3) admits only those individual remarks that are themselves self-inculpatory. Collateral statements within a broader confession are not admissible. Harris's admission that he knew of the cocaine qualified. His statements blaming Williamson did not. Remanded. Why it matters: accomplice statements that shift blame get special suspicion.

segments.ask: A shooting victim, bleeding heavily, says, I'm dying, Joe shot me, then recovers but moves abroad and cannot be found. In Joe's attempted-murder prosecution, is it a dying declaration?
segments.answer: No. 804(b)(2) applies only in homicide prosecutions or civil cases. Attempted murder is not a homicide prosecution. Consider an excited utterance instead.

segments.ask: Same statement, the victim dies, homicide prosecution. Admissible?
segments.answer: Yes, if he believed death was imminent, the statement concerns its cause, and he is unavailable by death.

segments.ask: An accomplice tells police, I drove the car, but Mike did the shooting. Under Williamson, what comes in against Mike?
segments.answer: Only the self-inculpatory part, I drove the car, and only if it is relevant. The part blaming Mike is collateral and not admissible under 804(b)(3).

segments.ask: A third party confesses to the crime a defendant is charged with. The defendant offers it under 804(b)(3). What extra requirement applies?
segments.answer: In a criminal case, corroborating circumstances clearly indicating trustworthiness, considering the totality of circumstances and any evidence supporting or undermining it.

segments.ask: A defendant has her husband killed to stop him testifying. What happens to her hearsay objection to his statements?
segments.answer: She forfeits it under 804(b)(6), if the wrongdoing and intent are proved by a preponderance.

segments.say: Traps. One: dying declarations only in homicide or civil cases. Two: settled hopeless expectation of imminent death. Three: 804(b)(3) is judged by a reasonable person. Four: only the self-inculpatory parts under Williamson. Five: corroboration in criminal cases applies to statements offered by either side. Six: forfeiture requires intent to cause unavailability.

Recap. 804(b)(2): homicide or civil, believing death imminent, about cause or circumstances. 804(b)(3): so contrary to interest a reasonable person would only say it if true, plus corroboration in criminal cases. 804(b)(6): wrongdoing intending unavailability. 806: attack the declarant as if a witness. Shepard, Williamson, Gray.

segments.ask: Name the three interests in 804(b)(3).
segments.answer: Pecuniary or proprietary interest, invalidating the declarant's claim against someone else, and exposure to civil or criminal liability.

segments.ask: What did Mrs. Shepard lack?
segments.answer: A settled hopeless expectation of imminent death.

segments.ask: Under Rule 806, is the 613(b) foundation needed to impeach a hearsay declarant?
segments.answer: No.

episodes.title: 803(1) to (3): present sense impression, excited utterance, and state of mind

segments.say: Roadmap. The first three 803 exceptions, which apply whether or not the declarant is available, the personal knowledge requirement, Judge Posner's doubts, the Hillmon doctrine, and Pheaster.
803(1), present sense impression. A statement describing or explaining an event or condition, made while or immediately after the declarant perceived it. The rationale: no time to fabricate.

803(2), excited utterance. A statement relating to a startling event or condition, made while the declarant was under the stress of excitement that it caused. The rationale: stress stills reflection. Contrast the two: 803(1) requires describing and timing; 803(2) requires only relating to, but requires stress.
Personal knowledge applies to declarants. The Advisory Committee Note says so, and the slides use a clip from The Graduate.

Judge Posner's critique. In United States v. Boyce, Seventh Circuit, 2014, concurring, he doubted both 803(1) and 803(2). Most lies are spontaneous, so lack of time to reflect does not guarantee truth. And excitement impairs perception.

803(3), then-existing mental, emotional, or physical condition. A statement of the declarant's then-existing state of mind, such as motive, intent, or plan, or emotional, sensory, or physical condition, such as mental feeling, pain, or bodily health. But not including a statement of memory or belief to prove the fact remembered or believed, unless it relates to the validity or terms of the declarant's will.
So: I am afraid, I intend to go to Denver, my back hurts, these are in. I remember that he hit me, offered to prove he hit me, is out. The exception: statements of memory about one's own will.
The Hillmon doctrine. A statement of the declarant's own intent may prove that the declarant later acted on it. Using it to prove another person's conduct is contested.

Mutual Life Insurance Company v. Hillmon, 1892. The insurers claimed the body was not Hillmon but a man named Walters. They offered Walters's letters saying he expected to leave Wichita with a certain Mr. Hillmon.

Held: the letters were admissible to show that Walters intended to go, and to go with Hillmon, which made it more probable that he did both. Why it matters: it is the source of the state-of-mind-to-prove-conduct rule, and of its third-party problem. As the slides put it, the letter could show Walters went. But showing that Hillmon went depends on Walters's memory of Hillmon's plan. That is a backward-looking memory, which 803(3) excludes.

United States v. Pheaster, Ninth Circuit, 1976, Fisher Problem 7.32. Before he disappeared from a restaurant parking lot, Larry Adell told his date and a friend he was going to meet Angelo there to pick up marijuana. Angelo Inciso was charged with kidnapping him.

Held: the Ninth Circuit admitted the statements under Hillmon, including to show that Inciso was there, despite the House report's view that 803(3) proves only the declarant's own conduct. Why it matters: it's the third-party Hillmon problem. Some courts require independent evidence of the other person's involvement.
